items.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019
items.q: I got to know a wonderful classical clarinetist in New York named Paul Garment.

ctx.x: jokingly, I said like, “Hey man” I said, “you know, you know what you need, you need a big band.” I said, like I did for, you know, like I said, joking, a big band with Bobby Short. Well I got a phone call from him about six months later saying, “You know you mentioned a band and you know, I can’t afford a big band.” I said, “I was just joking, Bobby, Jesus, you know.” He said, “Well I’ll tell you what, I have one gig” at some hotel, not the Carlyle but like a one night off gig, and I have some charts, and I’ve…

a great pianist. People said oh he rushed or he didn’t have a jazz feel. Who cares what he did. He was a brilliant orchestrator. Monk you would love this. He could sit down, like you could ask him to play a tune he hadn’t played in thirty years. He’d sit down and he’d play and he’d find his key, and what would come out of the piano would sound like a Billy Strayhorn arrangement. I mean he spontaneously could do that. I mean and he loved Ellington I mean that was his whole life was Ivy Anderson and Duke Ellington…

explain. But he was a Brooklyn liberal guy who wound up in the Nixon White House and became a real, I guess what you’d call eminence grise in Washington in the 70s days with Pat Moynihan at the U.N. and was a real culturally, he loved culture. And through the mechanisms of Washington and politics of lobbying and politics he wound up doing a lot of great things. The National Endowments for the Arts and Humanities, which were created during the Nixon administration, excuse me, during the Johnson administration,…
